newsitem.title: USA: Boston Ed/C-TEC deal a model for other utilities.
newsitem.headline: Boston Ed/C-TEC deal a model for other utilities.

text.p: Utlity analysts on Monday said they saw the joint venture between Boston Edison and C-TEC Corp subsidiary RCN, Inc as a model for other utilities seeking new revenue growth as electricity deregulation looms.

Noting Massachusetts utilities "are on the fast track to deregulation," Barry Abramson of Prudential Securities Research said: "I would bet all the utilities are examining future partnerships that would make use of the assets they already have."
He noted that Boston Edison, which has the fourth largest fiber-optic network in the state, uses only 10 to 20 percent of that network.
"That leaves 80 to 90 percent of that network available for partners," said Abramson, who has a hold on Boston Edison.

Douglas Fischer of A.G. Edwards said: "There are a number of different ways electric utilities can take advantage of their strengths -- their fiber optic networks, their right of ways -- and this is one of them."
A.G. Edwards has a reduced position rating on Boston Edison because of the onset of deregulation, which is scheduled to begin in Massachusetts in January 1998.
"The proof of the pudding will be in how they will exploit these assets and when your talking about an investment this size, making sure you get a fair return," Fischer said.
Abramson found one of the more interesting aspects of the venture was its challenge to the local telephone company, NYNEX.

At a press conference, C-TEC CEO David McCourt told reporters that a two-week-old Yankee Group survey showed 70 percent of consumers would switch carriers "for a small discount on cable alone" and vowed to provide better quality service for less.
The new venture was taking on "two established players -- One with a 100 year old network and the other 20-to-30 year old network," McCourt said.
May, in an interview afterwards, said there are 1.6 million Boston Edison customers and he expected the new venture would capture about 30 percent of the market, but declined to give a timetable.
C-TEC gets access to Boston Edison's fibre optics network, which spans more than 200 miles and also gains the utilty's right of ways so that it can build out later.
